summary: Describes fault tolerance for the Label Distribution Protocol. MPLS is used in core networks where downtime must be minimal, so routers may use fault tolerant hardware or software, and this document covers how LDP's state can be preserved when parts fail.

eli5.summary: Big networks cannot afford to stop. This note explains how the label-handing system can keep working when part of the equipment breaks.

questions: how does ldp recover after tcp failure
what is the ldp ft reconnect flag
subtitle: Extensions that let MPLS label state survive a failed TCP connection between LDP peers.

tldr.problem: LDP says that when its TCP connection fails the router must tear down the label paths of the session, and messages lost in the failure can leave label state unknown, which hurts routers built for high availability.
tldr.mechanism: Peers negotiate FT support in the Initialization message, number and acknowledge label messages (or check-point with Keepalive), keep state for a reconnection timeout, and re-issue unacknowledged messages once the connection returns.
tldr.outcome: Label state can be recovered without a full refresh, but an IESG Note warns that the timer guidance is weak and that the design should not be a model for TCP fault tolerance elsewhere.

today: RFC 3479 is a Proposed Standard, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. Its own IESG Note says it should not serve as a model for later TCP fault tolerance designs. A related approach for relearning state from the network is in RFC 3478.

sections.title: Why LDP Needs Fault Tolerance
sections.content:
Equipment vendors claim High Availability when hardware reaches at least 99.999% availability. To get there, a system fails over from a primary to a backup copy of hardware or software, with minimal disruption to the data plane. MPLS is meant for core networks where downtime must be kept to an absolute minimum.

LDP runs over TCP, and TCP makes some LDP messages (for example Label Release) unacknowledged. Plain LDP says that if the TCP connection fails, the LSR should immediately tear down the LSPs of the session and release their labels and resources. A fault tolerant TCP is described as notoriously hard, and messages lost in a failover may leave LSP or label state lost.

The RFC limits its scope to preserving label state between two adjacent LSRs. End-to-end LSP protection needs other techniques, and the document does not cover rerouting or layer 2 or layer 3 protection switching.
sections.eli5: Big networks must not stop. Today, if the link between two routers breaks, they throw away all the label notes they exchanged, even if the picture on the road never changed.

sections.title: Negotiating FT in the Initialization Message
sections.content:
Peers agree to use the LDP FT enhancements through a new FT Session TLV in the LDP Initialization message. Its S bit means sequence-numbered FT operations are supported, and its C bit means check-pointing is wanted. They can be set independently. The enhancements are used only if both peers include the TLV and agree on the S or C setting. If a peer uses them otherwise, the receiver treats it as a serious protocol error and ends the session.

An LSR that does not support any of this ignores the TLV, so sessions with it do not use FT. An LSR may behave as FT or non-FT on successive TCP connections between the same peers.

The TLV also carries an FT Reconnection Timeout, the longest time the sender will preserve FT label state after a TCP failure. Both peers use the lesser of the two proposed values, with zero treated as infinite.
sections.eli5: Before relying on the note-taking trick, both helpers must say they know it. If only one does, they use the old way.

sections.title: Acknowledging, Preserving and Re-issuing
sections.content:
A label becomes a Sequence Numbered FT Label when its first Label Request or Label Mapping carries an FT Protection TLV; every later message about it MUST carry one too. The FT sequence number goes up by one for each such message on the session. The receiver MUST secure the message (or the state it implies) and then ACK it with an FT ACK TLV, but not necessarily at once. ACKs are cumulative, so one ACK for 4 covers 1 to 4, and they MUST NOT be sent out of sequence.

When the TCP connection fails, both peers SHOULD keep the state and resources for FT labels and start a reconnection timer. The RECOMMENDED default is 5 seconds. Operations that arise during the outage MUST be pended and run after reconnection, unless the LSR cannot pend them, in which case it must act as if the timer expired. Non-FT labels are released as plain LDP says.

After reconnection, each side sets the FT Reconnect flag to say whether it kept state. If both set it, they re-issue unacknowledged messages, skipping net-zero pairs such as a Label Request followed by a Label Abort. If either clears it, both release the old state.
sections.eli5: Each note gets a number, and the listener says "got up to number 12". If the line drops, they check the last number heard and resend only what was missed.

sections.title: Check-Pointing and Graceful Shutdown
sections.content:
Check-pointing lets a peer acknowledge only on request instead of per message. A Keepalive carrying an FT Protection TLV asks the receiver to flush acknowledgement of all earlier check-pointable messages, and the receiver MUST ACK once they are secured. With only the C bit set, no label is sequence numbered and all labels are check-pointable. This suits stable sessions such as targeted LDP sessions that can risk losing the most recent exchanges.

For planned events such as a software upgrade, a Keepalive can also carry an FT Cork TLV. Each side acknowledges the other's state in a three-way handshake, then stops sending label and address messages, and the session ends with a Temporary Shutdown Notification that, unlike plain Shutdown, does not clear state.
sections.eli5: Instead of saying "got it" after every sentence, one helper can ask at the end, "Did you save everything so far?" before a planned break.

sections.title: New TLVs and Status Codes
sections.content:
The FT Session TLV (0x0503, length 12) holds a 16 bit flags field, a reserved field, an FT Reconnect Timeout in milliseconds and a Recovery Time. The flags are R (reconnect), S (save state), A (all labels protected), C (check-pointing) and L (learn from network, using RFC 3478). It is invalid for S, C and L all to be zero, or for L to be set together with S or C.

The FT Protection TLV (0x0203, length 4) holds a 32 bit sequence number that starts at 0x00000001. The FT ACK TLV (0x0504, length 4) holds the cumulative ACK number, set to 0 if no FT operations were received. The FT Cork TLV (0x0505) has length 0. Ten new status codes report errors such as a missing or unexpected TLV, an ACK sequence error and exhausted sequence numbers.
sections.eli5: The note adds a few new labelled slips to LDP messages: one that says "I can do this", one that numbers a note, one that says "got it up to here", and one that says "let's pause".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Because peers can resume without re-exchanging all label attributes, new denial-of-service attacks are possible. An intruder posing as a peer can force a TCP failure and reconnect without the Reconnect flag, which forces all FT labels to be released. An intruder could also set the flag without keeping state, or interfere with the FT settings. The RFC says these can be countered by authentication between LDP peers, such as the MD5-based scheme in RFC 3036.

A second risk is using a label after the session that created it has ended. A downstream LSR might reuse the label while the upstream LSR still sends data with the old meaning. To limit this, the RFC requires that a label not be reused until the Reconnection Timeout has expired.
sections.eli5: A bad actor could trick two routers into forgetting their notes, or make them use an old label for a new road. Passwords between routers and a waiting period before reusing labels help.

sections.title: The IESG Note
sections.content: The front page carries an IESG Note. It says the specification covers detecting failure and failing over a TCP connection carrying LDP control traffic to a new connection, but is not a general approach to using multiple TCP connections for fault tolerance. It lacks adequate guidance on timer and retry values, should not be a model for future TCP fault tolerance designs, and users are advised to test configurations very carefully for problems such as premature failovers.
sections.eli5: The people who approved this note said, "This works for LDP, but test it carefully and do not copy it blindly."

viz.caption: FT FLAGS IN THE FT SESSION TLV (RFC 3479 SECTION 8.2)

items.label: FT Reconnect
items.desc: Sender preserved state and resources for all FT labels since the previous session.

items.label: Save State
items.desc: FT Protection TLV is used beyond check-pointing; some labels may be sequence numbered.

items.label: All-Label Protection
items.desc: All labels MUST be treated as sequence numbered. Only meaningful if S is set.

items.label: Learn From Network
items.desc: Recovery procedures of RFC 3478 are used to relearn state.
